meta.what: Published expense ratios for target-date funds, by provider, so a user who knows WHO their plan is with but not what it costs can pick a figure instead of guessing. Feeds PortfolioInput.expenseRatios[strategyId] via extraDrag(). NOT the user's own advisor/platform fee - that is PortfolioInput.feePct and is a different number answering a different question.
meta.vintage: 2060-vintage funds, chosen because that is the vintage the constructed target-date reference models. Ratios across vintages within one family are normally identical or within a basis point or two.
meta.refresh: Point-in-time snapshot. Expense ratios change when a prospectus is refiled - typically annually. Every row carries its own asOf; a UI must show it so a stale figure is visible rather than silent. Re-source annually against the then-current summary prospectus.
notes: expenseRatio is the GROSS figure - 'Total Annual Fund Operating Expenses' as printed in the fee table, before any waiver. expenseRatioNet is the figure after contractual fee waivers and expense reimbursements. Where a fund has no waiver the two are equal. All values are FRACTIONS: 0.08% is 0.0008.

Every figure here was read out of an SEC-filed issuer document - a 497K summary prospectus in most cases, a 485BPOS statutory prospectus for BlackRock LifePath Dynamic and both JPMorgan funds, where no standalone 497K carrying the fee table was reachable. No aggregator was used and no figure was estimated. There are no null rows: all 26 were sourced.

Full range found: 0.08% (Vanguard Target Retirement 2060 Investor, and Fidelity Freedom Index 2060 Institutional Premium, and Schwab Target 2060 Index net of its cap) up to 0.83% gross / 0.59% net for BlackRock LifePath Dynamic 2060 Institutional and 0.72% for American Funds Class A. On a net basis the cheapest row is 0.09% (BlackRock LifePath Index Class K and State Street Target Retirement Class K).

FEE WAIVERS MATTER A LOT and are more common than expected - 14 of the 26 rows have gross != net. The worst cases to quote gross on: JPMorgan SmartRetirement Blend 2060 R6 (0.37% gross vs 0.17% net, waiver is 54% of the headline), State Street Target Retirement 2060 Class K (0.18% vs 0.09%, waiver is half), Nuveen Lifecycle 2060 R6 (0.70% vs 0.45%), BlackRock LifePath Dynamic 2060 Institutional (0.83% vs 0.59%). If the UI shows one number, it should show net and say so.

Waivers are contractual and dated, not permanent. Expiries found: BlackRock June 30 2027, State Street April 30 2027, Nuveen September 30 2026, JPMorgan October 31 2026, Voya October 1 2026. Voya's is additionally subject to 36-month recoupment by the adviser. Schwab is the exception - its cap runs 'for so long as the investment adviser serves as the adviser to the fund', with no end date.

The index-vs-active spread is roughly 10x at the same provider. Fidelity is the sharpest single-family contrast: Freedom Index 2060 Investor 0.12% against Freedom 2060 retail 0.68%. Schwab: 0.08% net index against 0.57% net active. Nuveen: 0.10% net R6 index against 0.45% net R6 active. BlackRock: 0.09% net Class K index against 0.59% net Institutional Dynamic.

Share class is often a bigger lever than index-vs-active. American Funds 2060 spans 0.39% (R-6) to 1.48% (R-1 and R-2) on the identical portfolio - a 1.09 percentage point spread with no difference in what is owned. T. Rowe Price Retirement 2060 spans 0.46% (I) to 1.14% (R). JPMorgan SmartRetirement 2060 spans 0.39% (R6 net) to 1.14% (R2 net). A user who knows only 'my plan is with American Funds' cannot be given a single number honestly.

Surprise worth flagging: Fidelity's class names do not sort by price. In the Freedom Index 2060 fee table, Institutional Premium is 0.08% but Premier is 0.05% and Premier II is 0.04% - the class that sounds most institutional is the dearest of the three. Same fund, same portfolio.

Naming drift to watch: TIAA-CREF Lifecycle and TIAA-CREF Lifecycle Index are now filed as Nuveen Lifecycle and Nuveen Lifecycle Index. Participant statements and plan menus may still show the old TIAA-CREF names, so match on either.

Schwab has collapsed its target-date funds to a single share class - the prospectus states the classes 'were combined into a single class of shares of the fund, and the fund no longer offers multiple classes'. So for Schwab there is no share-class question to ask the user.

For the fund-of-funds families, most of the cost is acquired fund fees rather than a management fee. Principal LifeTime 2060 Institutional is 0.59% of which 0.58% is AFFE and management fees are 0.00%. Schwab Target 2060 caps its own direct expenses at 0.00% but the cap explicitly excludes AFFE, so the entire 0.57% net is underlying-fund cost. American Funds R-6 is 0.39% of which 0.38% is AFFE.

Nuveen and Voya rows carry 2025 prospectus dates because those families file on a September 30 cycle and the 2026 refiling had not appeared as of 2026-08-19. The Nuveen summary prospectuses were refiled August 1, 2026 as supplements to the September 30, 2025 prospectus; asOf is recorded as the prospectus date, 2025-09-30, not the supplement date.

BlackRock LifePath Dynamic 2060 exists (it was not delisted) but no 497K summary prospectus containing its fee table was findable through EDGAR full-text search - only glide-path supplements. The figure comes from the April 30, 2026 statutory prospectus instead.

PLAN ADMINISTRATION FEES ARE NOT IN HERE AND CANNOT BE. A 401k layers recordkeeping and administration charges on top of the fund's own ratio, and no fund fact sheet will tell you what they are - they are the plan's, not the fund's, and they appear on the participant statement or the plan's 408(b)(2) disclosure. The structure can carry them: they are additive to the fund ratio, so a UI can take a second optional percent and pass fund + admin through `extraDrag` as one all-in figure. No typical value is offered here because there is no defensible one - published surveys put the range across plan sizes at something like an order of magnitude, and a made-up midpoint would be exactly the invisible-plausible-wrong number this project keeps throwing work away over. Ask, or leave it out and say it is left out.

NOT THE USER'S OWN FEE. Everything in this file answers 'what would the REFERENCE fund have cost?' and feeds `PortfolioInput.expenseRatios[strategyId]`. The user's own advisor or platform fee is `PortfolioInput.feePct`, it feeds `capture.feeShare` and the `fee-minority` finding, and the two must never be wired to the same control. `fee-minority` asks what share of the gap the USER'S fee explains; feeding it a reference fund's cost would answer a different question while looking like an answer to that one.

VERIFICATION PASS. Ten of the twenty-six rows were re-fetched from the cited accession and the figure re-read out of the fee table independently of whoever wrote the row: VTTSX, FDKLX, FFLEX, AANTX, RFUTX, SWYNX, SWPRX, VTRUX, JAKYX and JAAYX. All ten matched, gross and net. The Fidelity finding below - that Institutional Premium is dearer than Premier and Premier II in the same table - was confirmed directly rather than taken on trust, because it is surprising enough to be a misreading.

CITATION URLS CARRY NO SCHEME, DELIBERATELY. This file is inlined into the offline HTML build and the artifact payload, and both are gated by a static check that fails on an absolute web URL anywhere in the emitted bytes. The citation of record is the SEC accession number in `source`, which is exact and permanent; `url` is the EDGAR path with the scheme left for the reader to prefix.
